mcq.q: 10 M registered users means you need…
options: 10 M concurrent requests of capacity, one per user
Unknown until you know active use, peaks and task time
About 1 M requests per second at the busiest minute
Nothing yet, since users will arrive slowly at first
mcq.why: Load comes from active users, peak behaviour and request cost, not registrations.
distractors: Few registered users are active at once.
There is no basis for this without usage data.

mcq.q: 50 RPS with 8 s average time in system gives about how many in flight?
mcq.why: Little's law: L = λW = 50 × 8 (an average, not a p99).
distractors: That divides 50 by 8 instead of multiplying.
That is the arrival rate, not the number in flight.
That is ten times too many.

mcq.q: 2 million daily active users × 4 requests, 15% in the peak hour, burst factor 3. What is peak RPS?
options: About 333
About 8,000
About 1,000
About 93
distractors: That leaves out the burst factor.
That is requests per day in thousands.
That divides by 86,400 and skips the peak share.

mcq.q: Little's law gives which number?
options: The p99 concurrency during bursts
The average in flight, for a stable system
The peak burst in a single minute
The number of users online at once
mcq.why: Concurrency = arrival rate × time in system, an average; plan headroom above it.
distractors: It gives an average, not a tail.

mcq.q: A team puts p99 latency into Little's law. What is wrong?
options: It should use the p50 arrival rate instead
It needs tokens per request, not seconds
Nothing; p99 is the safer input to use
It uses average time in system; p99 overstates it
mcq.why: Use the average time; handle tails with headroom.
distractors: The arrival rate is not the issue.
Time in system is in seconds.

mcq.q: Arrival rate 7/s, mean service time 0.5 s, 4 servers. What is utilisation?
options: About 14%
About 88%
About 50%
About 350%
distractors: That forgets to divide by c.

mcq.q: What happens to queue waits as utilisation approaches 100%?
options: They stay constant
They explode
They become zero
They fall
mcq.why: Below about 80% queues stay short; near 100% waits grow fast.

mcq.q: Average RPS × a peak factor of (peak-hour share × 24 × burst) equals…
options: The average concurrency in flight
The same peak RPS as the hour formula
Double the hour-based peak RPS
The total requests for the day
mcq.why: Both forms are equivalent; do not apply the peak factor twice.
distractors: Concurrency also needs time in system.

mcq.q: Where should background work such as re-embedding and evaluation runs be scheduled?
options: Inside user requests
At the peak hour
Never
Away from peaks
mcq.why: Background work competes with interactive traffic.

mcq.q: Peak output demand: 100 RPS × 350 output tokens each. What is it?
options: 3,500 tokens/s
350,000 tokens/s
35,000 tokens/s
100 tokens/s
mcq.why: 100 × 350 = 35,000 tokens per second.
distractors: That is ten times too many.

mcq.q: An AI feature has 200,000 daily active users making 6 requests a day. 12% of requests fall in the peak hour, with a burst factor of 2. What is the peak RPS?
options: About 80
About 14
About 40
About 160
mcq.why: 200,000 × 6 × 0.12 ÷ 3,600 = 40 per second in the peak hour, × 2 for the burst.
distractors: That leaves out the burst factor.
That applies the burst factor twice.

mcq.q: A cheap model succeeds 62% at $0.004; failures cost $4 of human time. Per success it costs about…
distractors: That is the cost per attempt divided by the success rate, ignoring human cost.
That leaves out most of the human cost.
That is the human cost of one failure alone.

mcq.q: Why is cost per request misleading?
options: Requests are free with most providers, so it reads zero
It always overstates the real cost of serving users
It is too hard to compute for teams in practice
Retries, failures and escalations cost money without value
mcq.why: Cost per successful task ties cost to value.
distractors: It is easy; it is just misleading.

mcq.q: Option B costs $0.011 per attempt, succeeds 91%, and failures cost $4 of human time. Cost per success?
options: About $0.012
About $0.36
About $0.41
About $4.01
distractors: That forgets to divide by the success rate.
That counts a failure for every task.

mcq.q: $10 is spent on 100 tasks and 50 succeed. What is the cost per successful task?
mcq.why: $10 / 50 = $0.20, plus the support cost of the failures.

mcq.q: Choose all the costs to include in cost per successful task.
options: Model tokens and embeddings
The office rent of unrelated teams
Human review
Retrieval infrastructure and tools
mcq.why: Include the full cost of delivering the task.

mcq.q: Spend rose 40% with flat traffic. What helped find the cause?
options: Cost attribution by feature and tenant
Ignoring it until traffic grows
Raising every team's budget
Switching to another provider
mcq.why: One tenant called summarise on every page view (17.5).
distractors: The cause was one tenant's usage.

mcq.q: At what budget levels does the chapter suggest alerts?
options: Never; budgets should stop spend silently
Only at 100%, when the limit is hit
At every single percent of spend
mcq.why: At the limit, degrade or block per contract.
distractors: Teams need warning before limits bite.
That is too late to act.

mcq.q: What should capacity forecasting add beyond growth trends?
options: Random noise to stress-test the plan
Known events: launches, big customers, seasons
Nothing beyond the long-run growth trend
Last week's traffic, repeated each week
mcq.why: Order GPUs or raise quotas with lead time.
distractors: Noise is not a forecast input.
One week misses seasons and launches.

mcq.q: Where are budgets enforced?
options: Only in the system prompt of each app
Only per model provider, on its invoice
Only once, at the end of each month
Per request, task, user, tenant, feature
mcq.why: Layered limits catch runaway use early.
distractors: Tenants and features need limits too.

mcq.q: A cheaper model has a lower success rate. Can it cost more per success?
options: Only if its tokens are free
No, never, since it is cheaper
Only for agent tasks, not chat
Yes, once failures and escalations count
mcq.why: That is the point of the metric.
distractors: Free tokens do not remove human cost.

mcq.q: Option B costs $0.02 per attempt and succeeds 90% of the time; each failure costs $4 of human time. What is its cost per successful task?
options: About $0.47
About $0.022
About $0.42
About $4.02
distractors: That is 0.02 ÷ 0.90, ignoring the human cost of failures.
That forgets to divide by the success rate.
That adds a whole failure to every task.

mcq.q: What is the difference between an SLI and an SLO?
options: An SLO is the contract signed with customers
They are the same measurement, under two names
An SLI is a measure; an SLO is its target over a window
An SLI is the target the service must reach
mcq.why: SLA is the contractual promise, usually looser.
distractors: One measures; the other is a target.

mcq.q: An SLO of 99.9% over 140 million requests a month allows how many failed requests?
Each extra “nine” in an SLO changes the error budget how?
options: Cuts it tenfold
Halves it each time
Leaves it unchanged
Doubles the budget
distractors: Each nine divides the allowed failure by ten, not two.
A higher SLO shrinks the budget.

mcq.q: Why is an SLA usually looser than the internal SLO?
options: SLAs are not measured by anyone in practice
Because internal SLOs are optional for teams
So the team is warned before breaching the contract
Customers prefer a slightly worse service
mcq.why: The gap is a safety margin.
distractors: They are measured, often by customers.
The gap gives a safety margin.

mcq.q: Availability stayed at 99.95% while groundedness fell from 96% to 81% for three days. What would have caught it?
options: A stricter availability SLO, such as 99.99%
A cost SLO per resolved conversation
More replicas of the answer service
A daily sampled-quality SLO with an alert
mcq.why: Quality needs its own SLO (17.4).

mcq.q: What happens when the error budget is spent fast?
options: Alerts fire; risky releases freeze
Users are charged for the failures
The SLO target is raised to compensate
Nothing happens until the month ends
mcq.why: Budgets guide release decisions (17.8).
distractors: The point is to act early.

mcq.q: Which is a freshness SLI for RAG?
options: Cost per successful task
Groundedness of answers
Edit-to-searchable lag
Time to first token
mcq.why: e.g. p99 ≤ 10 minutes.

mcq.q: A sampled judge score is…
options: A measure of the service's availability
A contract signed with each customer
A complete measure of every answer given
An estimate from a sample, not all answers
mcq.why: State the sample and its limits.

mcq.q: A provider outage lasts 1 hour in a 30-day month. Roughly what share of the month is that?
options: About 1.4%, far over any budget
About 14% of the month
About 0.014%, well inside 99.9%
About 0.14%, over a 99.9% budget
distractors: That is ten times too much.
That is a hundred times too much.
That is ten times too little.

mcq.q: Which is a cost SLO from the chapter?
options: p95 TTFT ≤ 1.5 seconds
99.9% availability, monthly
Groundedness ≥ 95% daily
≤ $0.012 per resolved chat
mcq.why: Cost per successful task belongs in the SLO set.

mcq.q: A service handles 20 million requests a month with an availability SLO of 99.9%. How many failed requests does the error budget allow?
mcq.why: 0.1% of 20 million.

mcq.q: Why separate ingestion, retrieval, generation and agent workloads?
options: Different profiles and latency needs; one can starve the others
To use more servers in total, so each one runs cooler
To simplify billing so each team pays for its own servers
Because agent frameworks require separate clusters
mcq.why: e.g. a backfill saturating embedding GPUs used for query embeddings.
distractors: Separation is about isolation, not size.
Billing is a side benefit at most.

mcq.q: What latency does retrieval need, per the chapter's table?
options: About one second, for first token
Seconds to hours per task
Tens of milliseconds
Minutes, within a freshness SLO
mcq.why: Many small, RAM-heavy reads.

mcq.q: To cut GPU costs, a team wants to run some work on cheaper spot capacity that can be reclaimed at short notice. Which workload suits it?
options: Ingestion
Interactive generation
Agent approval steps
Retrieval
mcq.why: Ingestion is bulk and can retry; freshness SLOs are in minutes.

mcq.q: In the Monday example, why did search latency stay at 40 ms during a 2M-document re-ingestion?
options: Search was served from a cache only
The backfill was cancelled for the day
Employees did not use search that morning
Query and ingestion embeddings used separate pools
mcq.why: The backfill queue took longer, within its freshness budget.

mcq.q: What is the scaling unit for agent execution?
options: Workflow workers, own model quota
Queue consumers on spot capacity
Model replicas and nothing else
Index replicas for each tenant
mcq.why: Agents are long-running with durable state.

mcq.q: Services are split but share one unbounded queue and a saturated database. What happens?
options: Nothing; the services are separate
They can still starve each other
The shared queue limits the load
Latency improves for every service
mcq.why: Separation must cover shared dependencies too.

mcq.q: Long agent runs hold all model slots during peak chat. What fixes it?
options: A longer timeout for chat requests
More agents to finish runs faster
Disabling chat during agent runs
A separate model quota for agents
mcq.why: Agents draw from their own quota.

mcq.q: Which resource dominates ingestion?
options: CPU to parse and OCR, GPU to embed
RAM for reading the index fast
Streaming GPU decode per token
Durable workflow state storage
mcq.why: Bursty bulk work.

mcq.q: During a backfill, what should the assistant answer from?
options: Nothing until the backfill is done
Half-written chunks as they land
The last consistent index, showing its lag
A randomly chosen older index
mcq.why: Readers use published versions.

mcq.q: Which is the right isolation for query embeddings?
options: CPU only, to keep GPUs for ingestion
No embeddings at query time at all
The same pool as bulk ingestion
A small low-latency pool, separate from bulk
mcq.why: Query embedding is on the critical path.
distractors: Dense search needs a query vector.

mcq.q: Search query embeddings share a GPU pool with a 2-million-document backfill, and search p95 jumps from 40 ms to 900 ms. What fixes it?
options: Pause search until the backfill completes
Raise the backfill's priority so it finishes sooner
Run the backfill on the query pool at night only
Give query embeddings their own small low-latency pool
mcq.why: Latency-critical and bulk work need separate pools; the backfill then just takes longer.
distractors: Backfills often cannot wait, and the pools still collide.

mcq.q: A tenant's 2 million documents must be re-ingested within 2 hours. Each ingestion worker processes 50 documents per second. How many workers are needed, at minimum?
mcq.why: 2,000,000 ÷ 7,200 s ≈ 278 documents per second, ÷ 50 ≈ 5.6, so 6 workers.
distractors: That is the documents per second needed, not the workers.
That uses minutes instead of seconds somewhere.

mcq.q: Why make request handlers stateless?
options: To use less RAM on each replica of the service
Because databases are too slow to hold any state
Any replica can serve any request, so scaling is free
To avoid writing any logs for each request
mcq.why: State lives in databases.
distractors: Memory is not the main reason.

mcq.q: What belongs in a queue rather than in the user's request?
options: Streaming the generated tokens back to the user's browser
Authenticating the user before the request is accepted
Health checks that the load balancer sends every few seconds
Work that need not finish in the request, such as document processing
mcq.why: Queues give retries, backpressure and smoothing.
distractors: That must happen in the request.

mcq.q: Why is a semantic cache risky?
options: It needs GPUs to run its lookups
Similar is not identical: wrong answers
It is too slow to be worth using
It cannot store long answers
mcq.why: Restrict it to FAQ-style content and include tenant and permission scope.

mcq.q: An exact response cache returned tenant A's answer to tenant B, and kept serving old answers after a prompt update. Which fields should its key include? Choose all that apply.
options: Normalised prompt and prompt version
Tenant
The current time in seconds
Model and ACL scope
mcq.why: Key = hash(tenant, normalised prompt, model, prompt version, ACL scope).
distractors: That would make every key unique.

mcq.q: “How do I cancel my subscription?” and “How do I cancel my colleague's subscription?” hit the same semantic-cache entry. What is the lesson?
options: Lower the similarity threshold so more queries match
Similar queries need different answers; restrict and test it
Use a bigger embedding model to tell them apart
Cache every answer, since misses are costly
mcq.why: A tight threshold and FAQ-only scope reduce false hits.

mcq.q: When should a task use asynchronous UX?
options: Over ~30 s: task ID, progress, notify
Never; hold the connection open
Only when an error has occurred
Always, even for one-second tasks
mcq.why: Do not hold HTTP connections open for long tasks.

mcq.q: What must every cache have?
options: Invalidation tied to document updates
A GPU to compute its lookups fast
No keys at all, to keep it simple
An unlimited time to live per entry
mcq.why: Edits must purge stale answers (10.4).

mcq.q: Which store fits transactional state such as conversations and tasks?
options: A vector store built for embeddings
An in-memory cache on each CPU host
Object storage for documents and files
A transactional database such as Postgres
mcq.why: Choose stores per access pattern.

mcq.q: What share of requests does the figure suggest an exact cache hits?
options: About 5%
About 90%
About 50%
mcq.why: Exact repeats are rare; the cache is cheap but small.
distractors: It is small but not zero.

mcq.q: Never cache across…
options: Different user languages
Tenants or permission scopes
Model versions, nothing else
Different user time zones
mcq.why: A cached answer can leak data to another tenant.
distractors: Versions belong in the key, but tenants matter most.

mcq.q: A 3-minute report agent sits behind a synchronous HTTP endpoint, and the load balancer cuts requests at 60 seconds. What should the design be?
options: Retry the request automatically after each timeout
Raise the load balancer's timeout to ten minutes
Return a task ID at once, show progress and notify on completion
Shorten the report until it fits in 60 seconds
mcq.why: Tasks over about 30 s need asynchronous UX, not a held-open request.
distractors: Long-held connections still drop and waste resources.
The task needs its full time.

mcq.q: A policy document was updated, but cached answers kept quoting the old version for a day. What was missing?
options: A bigger cache so new answers fit in
Cache invalidation tied to document updates
A longer time to live for each entry
A semantic cache in front of the exact cache
mcq.why: Every cache needs invalidation when its source documents change.
distractors: Size does not remove old entries.
More caching does not remove stale entries.

mcq.q: What is a model gateway?
options: A shared prompt template that all the teams use
A central service between apps and all model backends
A vector index that several applications share
A type of GPU that is used for model serving
mcq.why: One API with credentials, routing, quotas, retries, caching, metering and policy.
distractors: Templates are content, not a service.

mcq.q: What happens without a gateway?
options: Costs fall, because no one adds an extra service hop
Models get faster without the extra network hop in front
Every team rebuilds quotas and fallbacks; no one sees total spend
Nothing changes for the teams that already call providers
mcq.why: A gateway centralises these concerns.
distractors: The hop is small; the gaps are large.
Each team rebuilds the same controls.

mcq.q: A gateway must send classification to a cheap model, keep EU tenants in the EU, and avoid a provider that is degraded. Which routing criteria does it need? Choose all that apply.
options: Tenant tier and region or residency
Load and provider health
The user's name
Task type
mcq.why: Routing by identity of a person is not a criterion.

mcq.q: How are tenant quotas typically enforced?
options: With token buckets on requests, tokens, concurrency, spend
By DNS records that point each tenant elsewhere
By asking tenants politely to slow down at peaks
By the model refusing requests once it is busy
mcq.why: Token buckets allow short bursts within limits.

mcq.q: Capacity 100 units/s. Tenants B–E send 15 each; tenant A normally sends 10 and bursts to 10×. What is total offered load?
options: 100 units/s, exactly the capacity
70 units/s, as A's burst is capped
250 units/s, counting A's burst twice
160 units/s, above capacity
mcq.why: 4 × 15 + 100 = 160 > 100, so FIFO waits grow for everyone.
distractors: A is not capped without quotas.

mcq.q: With per-tenant quotas and fair queuing, what happens to tenant A's burst?
options: A gets priority for its burst
The whole service crashes
A is throttled; others are unaffected
Everyone slows down equally
mcq.why: Fair queuing contains noisy neighbours.

mcq.q: Why can automatic fallback to another model be risky?
options: Fallbacks are always slower than the primary model
It is not allowed under most provider contracts
The fallback may handle tools and schemas differently
It uses many more tokens for each request it serves
mcq.why: Evaluate fallbacks for compatibility.
distractors: Tokens are not the main risk.

mcq.q: What is fairness when capacity is short?
options: The largest tenant goes first, always
Each tenant gets a fair share, weighted by tier
A random tenant is picked each time
First come, first served for everyone
mcq.why: FIFO lets one tenant's spike dominate.
distractors: Random is not fair by design.

mcq.q: Why weight quotas by estimated context size?
options: A huge context costs far more capacity
To simplify billing for tenants
Because tokens are free to serve
To favour tenants with long prompts
mcq.why: Request counts alone ignore cost differences.

mcq.q: Why must the gateway record usage per tenant and feature?
options: To train models on usage patterns
To slow requests down when busy
Because providers require it
So spend is visible and budgets enforced
mcq.why: Without central metering, nobody can see total spend.
distractors: Your own visibility is the reason.

mcq.q: Capacity is 100 units/s. Tenants B–E send 15 units/s each. With per-tenant fair queuing, roughly how much can tenant A use while it bursts to 100 units/s?
options: About 40 units/s, the capacity left after the others
About 20 units/s, an equal fifth of all capacity
About 100 units/s, the whole of its burst
About 10 units/s, its usual steady rate
mcq.why: B–E use 60 between them; fair queuing gives A the rest, so the others are unaffected.
distractors: Unused share is not wasted while others need less.
Spare capacity can serve part of the burst.

mcq.q: During a capacity shortage, an enterprise-tier tenant and a free-tier bulk script both send many requests. How should the gateway share capacity?
options: Weighted fair queuing by tier, within each tenant's quota
Largest tenant first, since it pays the most money
Randomly, so that no single tenant is favoured
First come, first served, whatever each tenant's tier
mcq.why: Fairness gives each tenant its share, weighted by tier, instead of first come, first served.
distractors: Random is not fair by design.
The bulk script would take everything.

mcq.q: During a provider slowdown, a gateway keeps accepting every request, and its queue grows to 40,000 items that mostly time out. What should it have done?
options: Push “slow down” upstream: bounded queues, 429 with Retry-After
Retried the slow requests faster and more often
Compressed the requests to save time on the network
Added servers and kept accepting all incoming work
mcq.why: Do not accept work you cannot finish in time.

mcq.q: A service is at twice its capacity. It serves paid chat, free-tier chat and overnight batch summaries. Which should it shed first?
options: Paid interactive requests
The newest requests regardless of priority
Random requests
The lowest priority: batch, then free tier
mcq.why: Shed early and cheaply so the rest succeed.

mcq.q: What does a circuit breaker do after the error rate crosses its threshold?
options: Retries harder against the failing provider to recover
Restarts the provider's service from the client side
Opens: calls fail fast or go to a fallback for a while
Disables logging to save time on each failed call
mcq.why: Then half-open trial calls decide whether to close.

mcq.q: In the half-open state, what happens?
options: All traffic goes through again at full rate
The breaker is removed from the path for good
A few trial calls test it: success closes, failure re-opens
No traffic goes through at all, as when open
mcq.why: Trial calls test recovery.

mcq.q: Why reject a request whose predicted wait exceeds its deadline?
options: To save space in the request logs
Because late requests are always malicious
To raise the service's SLO target
It would time out anyway, wasting GPU time
mcq.why: Deadline-aware shedding keeps capacity for requests that can succeed.

mcq.q: Which is lower on the degradation ladder than “mid model, same retrieval”?
options: Mid model, 4 chunks, no reranker, shorter
Two large models in parallel
Full service with every feature
Large model, 8 chunks and a reranker
mcq.why: L2 reduces retrieval and output after L1.

mcq.q: What should be done with each degradation level before an incident?
options: Nothing; decide during the incident
Delete it once the plan is written
Evaluate its quality; define when to switch
Hide it from the users entirely
mcq.why: Levels are defined in advance and switched automatically.
distractors: Levels must exist to be used.

mcq.q: Load is 1.6× capacity with no shedding. What happens?
options: The queue grows; many miss deadlines and work is wasted
All requests succeed, just more slowly than usual
The service gets faster as its caches warm up
Only batch requests fail, by design of the queue
mcq.why: Unbounded queues trade rejections for long delays.
distractors: Overload does not speed it up.

mcq.q: Choose all the steps on the chapter's degradation ladder.
options: Silently return guesses
Cached answers and search results only
Smaller model
Fewer retrieved chunks and no reranker
mcq.why: The final step is a clear status message, never silent guesses.

mcq.q: Shedding by predicted wait vs priority shedding: what does priority add in the chapter's figure?
options: It removes deadlines from requests
Paid-tier requests are admitted first
It rejects paid requests first
It accepts every request
mcq.why: Paid tier (30% of traffic) is admitted before others.

mcq.q: A provider starts timing out after 30 s on every call. Threads pile up waiting, and the whole assistant hangs. Which control prevents this?
options: A circuit breaker that opens and fails fast to a fallback
More replicas of the assistant service, started automatically
More retries for each call that times out, with backoff
Longer timeouts so that slow calls eventually finish
mcq.why: After the error threshold, calls fail fast instead of waiting on a dying provider.
distractors: New replicas hang the same way.
Retries add load to a failing provider.

mcq.q: A queue holds 600 requests and the service completes 20 per second. A new request arrives with a 10-second deadline. What should deadline-aware shedding do?
options: Hold it until the queue empties, then run it
Admit it, since 600 ÷ 20 is only about 3 s
Reject or degrade it now: the predicted wait is about 30 s
Admit it, since the queue is shorter than 1,000
mcq.why: 600 ÷ 20 = 30 s, longer than the 10 s deadline, so the work would be wasted.
distractors: It would miss its deadline anyway.
The rule compares wait with the deadline, not queue size.

mcq.q: What is the difference between active-active and active-passive?
options: Active-passive has more regions than active-active does
Active-active never needs to fail over when a region dies
Active-active: both serve; active-passive: a standby takes over
They are the same design, just with two different names
mcq.why: Active-active is more complex for data consistency.
distractors: Region count does not define them.
It still shifts traffic on failure.
They differ in who serves traffic.

mcq.q: What is RPO?
options: How much data you may lose
How fast you must recover service
Requests per operation served
A replication protocol between regions
mcq.why: RTO is recovery time.

mcq.q: Why is a replica not a backup?
options: Replicas copy corruption and deletes instantly
Replicas cannot be read during an outage
Backups are always faster to restore
Replicas are slower than the primary
mcq.why: Test restores on a schedule.

mcq.q: EU tenants' data must stay in the EU. Where can they fail over?
options: Only to EU capacity
Any region, nearest first
Nowhere; they wait it out
The US only, as the backup
mcq.why: Residency constrains failover targets.

mcq.q: Why replicate or snapshot vector indexes?
options: Regulations require snapshots
Rebuilding takes hours at scale
They are small and cheap to keep
They cannot be rebuilt at all
mcq.why: Rebuilding is possible but slow.

mcq.q: In the game-day example, what did the first run find?
options: The database was lost during the test and had to be restored
Everything worked exactly as planned on the first run
The primary provider was really down during the game day
The fallback ignored the schema in 4% of replies, and quota was short
mcq.why: Both would have surfaced during a real outage.

mcq.q: After a regional outage, traffic moves back to the primary region while writes queued during the failover are still pending. What must failback include?
options: Nothing; failback is automatic
Deleting the secondary region
Replaying queued writes exactly once
Replaying all writes twice
mcq.why: Rehearse failback too.

mcq.q: Active-active read-only search across regions is fine. Why do business actions need care?
options: Reads are slower across regions
Search is not replicated
Writes need one owner to avoid duplicates
Writes never fail, so no care is needed
mcq.why: Active-active does not give consistent business actions automatically.

mcq.q: How often should failover be tested?
options: Never, as the test itself is too risky
Once at launch, and never again after that
Only during real outages, when it matters
Regularly: untested failover usually fails
mcq.why: Regular game days find problems early.

mcq.q: What is RTO?
options: A token limit per request
How fast you must recover
How much data you may lose
The number of regions in use
mcq.why: RPO is the data-loss window.

mcq.q: A conversation store is backed up every 4 hours, with no other copy. Its RPO target is 1 hour. Is the target met?
options: Yes, because backups exist
No, because an RPO needs backups every minute
Yes, because a restore takes under an hour
No: up to 4 hours of data could be lost
mcq.why: RPO is how much data you may lose; backups every 4 hours can lose up to 4 hours.
distractors: Their interval sets the possible loss.
It needs them at least every hour.

mcq.q: The EU region fails. The nearest healthy region is in the US, but EU tenants' data must stay in the EU. Where should EU traffic go?
options: To the US region, since an outage overrides data residency
Only to other EU capacity, or to the degradation ladder if none is left
Nowhere: EU tenants should simply wait for the region to return
To whichever region has the lowest latency for those users
mcq.why: Residency constrains failover targets as well as normal routing.
distractors: Other EU capacity or degraded service can help.

mcq.q: Before launch, a team wants to know at what load its service breaks and whether load shedding kicks in. Which test answers that?
options: Unit test
Load test
Stress test
Soak test
mcq.why: Ramp beyond peak until SLOs fail.

mcq.q: Which test finds memory leaks and slow degradation?
options: Spike test
Soak test
Stress test
Smoke test
mcq.why: Moderate load for 8–24 hours.

mcq.q: Why do fixed 500-token prompts make a poor load test?
options: Fixed prompts cost more to send than prompts of varied lengths
Models reject repeated fixed prompts as a form of abuse
500 tokens is too long for a test, so the model times out
Real lengths are heavy-tailed: fixed prompts miss KV pressure and tails
mcq.why: Replay sampled production traces.
distractors: Length alone is not the problem.

mcq.q: What is coordinated omission?
options: Dropping error responses from the final load-test report
Two testers coordinating their runs so they do not overlap
Missing log lines on the server while it is under load
A closed-loop tester slows with the service, hiding latency
mcq.why: Use open-loop arrival rates.

mcq.q: What does a test against a mocked model validate?
options: Orchestration, queues and gateways only
Model-serving capacity on the GPUs
Nothing useful, since the model is fake
The quality of the model's answers
mcq.why: Real model capacity needs its own benchmark (14.7).

mcq.q: In the prompt-length figure, about what share of tokens do the top 10% of requests carry?
options: About 90%
Close to 40%
About 10%
About 1%
mcq.why: The long tail is where expensive requests live.

mcq.q: A marketing email will push traffic from 20% to 150% of capacity within a minute. Which test checks that autoscaling and queues absorb it?
options: Soak test
Load test
Spike test
Failure test
mcq.why: Checks autoscaling and queues absorb bursts.

mcq.q: Why use a mock for hosted APIs in load tests?
options: Mocks are more accurate than the real provider's API
Providers forbid any load testing against their API
To mimic latency and limits without cost or hitting limits
Mocks measure answer quality as well as latency
mcq.why: The mock must reproduce realistic distributions.

mcq.q: Your laptop runs both the load generator and the server. What do the numbers mean?
options: Little; it practises scenarios and percentiles
Exact GPU throughput for the production fleet
The provider's real rate limits under load
Production capacity, give or take a little
mcq.why: State the limitation.

mcq.q: Which k6 executor gives an open-loop test?
options: per-vu-iterations
a fixed number of virtual users each waiting for a response
ramping-arrival-rate
constant-vus
mcq.why: It sends requests at a set rate regardless of responses.

mcq.q: A closed-loop load test with 200 virtual users reports p95 latency of 1.2 s, but production at the same request rate sees 6 s. What is the likely cause?
options: p95 is always five times lower in tests
The test machine was too fast for the service
Coordinated omission: use an open-loop arrival-rate test
Production traffic was mocked incorrectly
mcq.why: The closed-loop tester slowed down with the service and hid queueing.
distractors: Speed of the tester is not the cause.
The test, not production, was mocked.

mcq.q: An 8-hour soak test at moderate load shows memory growing 1.5 GB an hour on each replica, with 16 GB of headroom. Roughly when will a replica run out?
options: After about 8 hours, when the test itself ended
After about 16 hours, the size of the headroom
After about 11 hours, within a day: a leak to fix
Never, since the test passed its full 8 hours
mcq.why: 16 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 10.7 hours, which a daily traffic cycle reaches.
distractors: The test ending is not the limit.
That ignores the 1.5 GB hourly growth rate.
The trend shows it will fail later.

mcq.q: Which kind of number is “one replica sustains 2,400 tok/s at p95 ITL 45 ms with our traffic mix (load test 2026-10-28)”?
options: A vendor claim
Actual production usage
Projected capacity
Measured performance
mcq.why: It comes from a test you ran, under stated conditions.

mcq.q: “12 replicas should support 30k output tok/s at peak” is…
options: Actual usage
A guarantee
Measured performance
Projected capacity
mcq.why: A calculation from measured numbers and assumptions.

mcq.q: What is actual production usage good for?
options: Ground truth for the past; input to forecasts
Marketing claims about how far it scales
Predicting any future load exactly
Replacing load tests entirely from now on
mcq.why: It describes what happened.
distractors: It is history, not a forecast.

mcq.q: A vendor said 5,000 tok/s per GPU. The team's own test with real prompts measured 1,700. Projected need was 20 GPUs from the vendor number. Roughly how many would the measured number imply for the same load?
options: About 34
About 59
About 7
About 20
mcq.why: 20 × 5,000 / 1,700 ≈ 59. Launch actually needed 52.

mcq.q: What procedural fix does the chapter recommend after that failed projection?
options: Trust vendors less, but keep their benchmark numbers in capacity plans
Plans cite measured numbers with conditions; launch reviews check them against actuals
Always add 10% to every projection as a buffer, whatever the source
Skip load tests and size the fleet from production telemetry later on
mcq.why: Label and compare all three kinds of number.
distractors: A fixed buffer would not have covered it.

mcq.q: Why does a measured number not transfer to another workload?
options: Hardware makes no difference to measured throughput
It holds only for the tested mix, hardware, conditions
Measurements expire after one day and must be redone
Measured numbers are always wrong for any workload
mcq.why: Change the mix and you must re-measure.
distractors: They are right for their conditions.

mcq.q: The actual peak crossed the safe limit and the forecast reaches projected capacity in two weeks. What should happen?
options: Remove the forecast from the dashboard
Lower the SLO to fit the capacity
Wait and see whether it holds
Add replicas or re-measure with today's mix
mcq.why: The projection may rest on an outdated load test.
distractors: The trend says it will not.

mcq.q: A simulation shows a design could serve 5 million users. How should it be described?
options: As measured performance
As production usage
As a projection, with its assumptions
As a system that served 5 million users
mcq.why: Never describe a simulation as real usage.
distractors: That claims what did not happen.

mcq.q: Which goes in a launch review statement?
options: “Same as the vendor benchmark for this GPU and model size”
“Fast enough for launch, based on the team's experience”
“Measured 60 RPS on staging at p95 1.8 s; 100 RPS projected, not validated”
“Handles millions of users, as other companies have shown”
mcq.why: Each figure is labelled with its kind and conditions.

mcq.q: “Peak last Monday: 18.2k output tok/s; p95 ITL 52 ms” is which kind of number?
options: A vendor benchmark
Actual production usage
Measured performance from a load test
Projected capacity
mcq.why: It comes from telemetry of real traffic.

mcq.q: Peak demand is forecast at 30,000 output tokens/s. One replica measured 2,400 tokens/s at the SLO with the real traffic mix. How many replicas, with one spare for redundancy?
options: 14: 13 for the load plus 1 spare
7, using a vendor figure of 5,000 tokens/s
13, which already rounds up the 12.5
12, since 12.5 rounds down

mcq.q: A slide says “our system handles 2,000 RPS”, from a staging load test against a mocked model. How should it be labelled?
options: Actual production usage, since the test ran on our own production code
Measured on staging, mocked model: orchestration only, not model capacity
Vendor benchmark, to be confirmed with the model provider before launch
Projected capacity, valid for production traffic exactly as it stands
mcq.why: Label the kind of number and its conditions; a mock does not test model serving.
distractors: It is a measurement with narrow conditions.
